title: Toldot: Esau's tears (Genesis 27:34–38)
hookLine: the tradition takes Esau's bitter cry seriously; his pain is written down

cards: Nobody films the losing team's locker room. The cameras are down the hall, with the champagne, and the kid on the bench with a towel over his head stays off the screen. Plenty of stories follow the winner out the door.

Jacob has just walked out of his father's tent with the blessing. Minutes later, Esau walks in, sweaty from the hunt, carrying the meal he cooked, saying: sit up, father, and eat, so you can bless me.
The Torah stays in that room.

teach.b: Isaac asks: who are you? I am your son, your firstborn, Esau. And the text says Isaac trembled, a great trembling, beyond measure.
Who was it, then, who came before you? I've blessed him, and he will stay blessed. Esau cries out, a great and bitter cry.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Bless me, even me also, O my father."
He asks again: "Hast thou but one blessing, my father?" And Esau lifts up his voice and weeps. Stop there for a moment.
This is the brother the story didn't choose, the one Rebekah didn't favor. The Torah could have skipped this scene. Instead it gives us his words, twice, and his tears.
Isaac does give him a blessing, a harder one: you'll live by your sword, and serve your brother, and one day you'll break his yoke from your neck. The rabbis didn't look away either.
An old midrash says Jacob made Esau cry out one bitter cry, and that cry was repaid generations later, in the book of Esther, when Mordecai too cried out with a loud and bitter cry.
That pain was not forgotten. It counted. There's a thread in Jewish tradition of taking the other side's suffering seriously, even the side you're told was not chosen.

At the Passover seder, there's a custom of spilling drops of wine from the cup as the plagues on Egypt are named, and one common explanation is that a full cup of joy shouldn't ignore someone else's pain.
But the Torah writes down the loser's tears.

how: Jewish teaching often turns to the suffering of the other side: at the Passover seder, it's a custom to spill drops of wine as each plague on Egypt is named, and the midrash on Esau's cry is taught alongside this story.

o: generations, a family's story over time
rivals, two brothers who fight for one prize
tears, the cry of the son who was left out

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: cried a great and bitter cry

s: it records his cry, his plea twice, and his tears.
Isaac gave Esau no blessing at all
he gave him a harder one: to live by the sword, and one day break his brother's yoke.
a midrash links Esau's cry to Mordecai's cry in Esther
the one bitter cry, the rabbis said, was not forgotten.

games.q: you're telling this story. Jacob has the blessing and walks out. what does your story do next?
o: stay in the room with Esau.
games.why: the Torah stays with Esau: his cry, bless me, even me also, and his tears. his pain is written down.

practice: Think of a time you won something, a job, an argument, a game, a place, and then of the person on the other side. Where were they that night, and what did it feel like to walk into the room too late?
You don't have to give anything back; just let their loss be real to you for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Toldot. Generations: the portion that ends with Esau's bitter cry, bless me, even me also, written down and not forgotten.

carryVoice: Your line: the loser's tears count. Esau's cry made it into the story. That's day one hundred ninety.

sources.q: Bless me, even me also, O my father.
